subtitle: Recognize the variety of religious and nonreligious life in Minnesota and plan services, meetings and accommodations that respect it without guessing.
audience: For all DHS and DSD employees, including case managers, policy and program staff, supervisors and anyone who plans meetings, services or events with Minnesotans of many faiths and none.

lessons.title: Religion in Minnesota public service and why it matters
objectives: Describe the broad shape of religious life in Minnesota using dated survey data and its limits.
Distinguish religion from ethnicity, language and national origin when planning services.
Explain why a public servant neither promotes nor dismisses anyone's faith or lack of faith.
Identify one question that invites a person to say what matters to them without predicting it.
lessons.teaching:
Minnesota is often described as a Lutheran and Catholic state, and there is truth in that picture. It is also incomplete. In the Pew Research Center's most recent Religious Landscape Study, about six in ten Minnesota adults identified as Christian: roughly one in five as evangelical Protestant, a little more than one in five as mainline Protestant, and a little under one in five as Catholic. About three in ten said they had no religious affiliation, a group that includes atheists, agnostics and people who say they are nothing in particular. Muslim, Jewish, Buddhist, Hindu and other Minnesotans appear as small shares in a statewide survey, and the margin of error of several points means small groups cannot be estimated precisely. Treat these numbers as a dated snapshot of the whole state, not a description of any town, team or person.

Religion is its own part of a person's life. It is related to ethnicity and peoplehood, and it is not the same thing. Islam is not Somali. The Black Church is not the whole of African American life. Lutheran Minnesota is not a polite way of saying white people; there are Hmong, Oromo and Latino Lutheran congregations. A convert is not an ethnicity. A person who left their congregation is still part of their family and people. When staff fold faith into culture, they tend to guess wrong in both directions: assuming belief that is not there and missing belief that is.

For DHS and DSD staff, faith can shape what a good service looks like: when appointments work, what food is acceptable at a meeting, who a family wants present when a hard decision is made, how illness, disability and healing are understood, and which days a provider or worker cannot be reached. Government employees serve people of every faith and of no faith. That means staff do not promote, discourage or rank religions, and they do not treat religious language as a sign that someone is refusing services. It also means they do not pretend religion is irrelevant when a person tells them it matters.

This course gives you a starting point, not a verdict. Each lesson names real variation inside traditions so that you ask better questions. The most useful habit is simple: ask the person what matters to them, record what they tell you, and let that answer, not a category, guide the plan.
lessons.keyPoint: Religion is its own part of a person's life, related to culture but not the same as it. Use statewide data as a dated snapshot and ask the person what matters.
lessons.example: Fictional case: Mariam, a DSD case manager, is preparing for a first home visit with a family whose referral lists their language as Somali. A colleague, Dale, suggests she schedule around Friday prayers and bring a list of mosques. Mariam notices that the referral says nothing about faith. At the visit she explains the service, then asks whether there are days, times or practices the team should plan around. The father says Friday afternoons are difficult. His adult daughter, who receives services, says she does not attend a mosque and wants her own schedule respected.
lessons.question: What should Mariam do next?
choices: Record the mosque list in the plan so the family has faith resources available.
Record both preferences in their own words and ask the daughter how she wants scheduling decided for her own services.
Avoid any mention of religion in the file so no one feels singled out.
feedback: The family did not ask for faith resources, and the daughter said she does not attend a mosque. Adding them treats a guess as a need.
This is the strongest response. It keeps what each person said, respects the daughter as the person receiving services, and lets her decide how family and faith fit into her plan.
Leaving it out loses useful scheduling information that the family chose to share. The goal is accuracy and respect, not silence.
lessons.reflection: Think about the religious or nonreligious assumptions built into the calendar and customs of your own workplace. Which ones feel so normal that you rarely notice them?
lessons.action: Review one intake form, meeting invitation or scheduling template you use. Mark any place where it assumes a religious calendar or practice, and draft one neutral question that lets a person tell you what to plan around.

check.question: How should staff use statewide survey data on religion in Minnesota?
check.correct: As a dated snapshot of the whole state that helps them expect variety, never as a prediction about an individual.
wrong: As a reliable guide to the religion of people in a given county or program.
As a reason to assume that anyone from a particular country shares that country's majority religion.
check.feedback: Statewide surveys describe large populations with margins of error, and small groups are hard to estimate. They help you expect variety. Only the person can tell you what their faith, or lack of faith, means for their services.

lessons.title: Christian traditions: Lutheran, Catholic, Black Church, Evangelical and Pentecostal
objectives: Distinguish the main Lutheran church bodies and explain why they are not interchangeable.
Describe Catholic Minnesota as many peoples organized through parishes and dioceses.
Explain why the Black Church is an institution with its own history and many denominations.
Identify at least four distinct evangelical and Pentecostal streams in Minnesota.
lessons.teaching:
Christianity is the largest religious identity in Minnesota, and its familiarity can make it invisible. Lutheran Minnesota grew from German, Norwegian, Swedish, Finnish and Danish immigration and later from Hmong, African and Latino congregations. The Evangelical Lutheran Church in America, the Lutheran Church Missouri Synod and the Wisconsin Evangelical Lutheran Synod are separate church bodies with different teaching on subjects such as the ordination of women. Baptism, confirmation, funerals and church basement coffee carry deep meaning for many families. Some staff meet a quiet habit of avoiding conflict and treating everyone the same, which can feel like fairness while hiding barriers. Naming that pattern is not a criticism of Lutheran faith; it is a reminder that an unmarked civic religion is still a religion.

Catholic Minnesota is many peoples: Irish, German, Polish, Czech, Italian, Mexican and other Latino, Vietnamese, Filipino, Congolese and more. The church is organized into the Archdiocese of Saint Paul and Minneapolis and the dioceses of Crookston, Duluth, New Ulm, Saint Cloud and Winona-Rochester. A parish can be a place of worship, mutual aid, school and trusted information. A Spanish-language Mass in a suburban parish and a long-established German parish in Stearns County are not one experience. When a family asks for a priest to be present, for example near the end of life, that is their request. Staff should not assign one.

The Black Church is an American institution with African and Christian roots, a long history of mutual aid, education and civil rights organizing, and a strong music tradition. It includes Baptist, African Methodist Episcopal, Church of God in Christ, nondenominational and other congregations, and many Black Minnesotans are Catholic, Muslim or unaffiliated. A Nigerian or Liberian Pentecostal congregation is not the same as a historic Northside or Rondo church. Titles such as Pastor, Deacon, Mother or Elder matter in many congregations. A phrase such as giving it to God describes faith and hope; it is not a refusal of services.

Evangelical and Pentecostal Minnesota is not one white suburban church. It includes white evangelical congregations, Black Pentecostal churches, Latino evangelical churches, Hmong Christian and Alliance congregations, Karen Baptist churches and many African immigrant churches, from metro campuses to small congregations in Greater Minnesota. Conversion, testimony and healing prayer are central for many. Across all these traditions the rule is the same: a pastor or priest is not the case plan unless the person asks for that role, and people who have left a church remain part of their families and communities.
lessons.keyPoint: Christian Minnesota is several traditions and many peoples. Name the church body, parish or congregation the person names, and let the person decide what role clergy play.
lessons.example: Fictional case: Gloria coordinates a person-centered planning meeting for Andre, a young man with a developmental disability who lives with his grandmother. His grandmother says she has prayed about the move to his own apartment and has given it to God. The provider representative, Kurt, writes in his notes that the family is resistant to the plan. Gloria notices that the grandmother has already asked practical questions about staffing and transportation. Andre says he wants his pastor to see the new apartment once he has moved in.
lessons.question: What should Gloria do next?
choices: Invite the pastor to lead the next planning meeting, since the family clearly relies on the church.
Ask Kurt to keep his note, because faith language often signals doubt about services.
Correct the note to reflect the grandmother's actual questions and add Andre's wish about his pastor as his own goal.
feedback: Andre asked for a visit to the apartment, not for his pastor to lead planning. Expanding the role goes beyond what he asked.
Faith language here expressed hope and trust. Recording it as resistance misreads the family and could bias later decisions.
This is the strongest response. The record reflects what was actually said, and Andre's request is treated as his goal, in his words.
lessons.reflection: When you hear someone use religious language about a decision, what meaning do you tend to give it? Where might that reading come from?
lessons.action: Look at one recent case note, meeting summary or provider report you wrote or reviewed. Check whether any description of faith or religious language is interpreted rather than quoted, and revise it to describe what the person actually said or asked for.

check.question: Which statement about Lutheran Minnesota is accurate?
check.correct: Several separate Lutheran church bodies, including the ELCA, the Missouri Synod and the Wisconsin Synod, have different teachings and practices.
wrong: Lutheran is mainly an ethnic label for Scandinavian Minnesotans.
Lutheran practice is essentially the absence of religion in public life.
check.feedback: Lutheran church bodies are distinct, and Lutheran congregations include Hmong, African, Latino and European American members. Treating Lutheran as an ethnicity or as neutral professionalism hides a real religious tradition that shapes many Minnesota workplaces.

lessons.title: Muslim and Jewish life in Minnesota
objectives: Describe the diversity of Muslim Minnesotans by origin, tradition and practice.
Distinguish Jewish religious movements and explain how religion and peoplehood relate.
Plan scheduling and service arrangements around prayer, fasting, Sabbath and holidays when a person asks.
Explain why antisemitism and anti-Muslim hostility are service and safety issues rather than matters of tone.
lessons.teaching:
Islam is a world religion, and Muslim Minnesotans include Somali, Oromo and other Ethiopian, Arab, South Asian, West African, Bosniak, African American and white convert communities, among others. Most are Sunni, and there are also Shia Muslims, Ahmadi Muslims and people whose families have roots in Black American Muslim movements; these are not interchangeable. Practice varies widely. Daily prayer, Friday congregational prayer, fasting during Ramadan, halal food and modesty in dress shape the working day for some Muslims and not for others. Arabic is a language of worship and is not automatically the language a person wants for an interview. Do not send someone to a Somali community resource because they are Muslim, and do not assume a Somali Minnesotan is observant.

Jewish Minnesota has deep roots in Minneapolis, Saint Paul, Duluth and the Iron Range, and includes Orthodox, Conservative, Reform, Reconstructionist and secular Jews, Israelis, and families who came from the former Soviet Union. Being Jewish is both a religion and a peoplehood; many Jews who do not practice religiously are still fully Jewish. Shabbat runs from Friday sundown to Saturday nightfall, and observant Jews may not use phones, drive or sign documents during it or during holidays such as Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and Passover. Kosher food rules and mourning customs such as sitting shiva can affect meetings and visits. A Russian-speaking Jewish family is not described by a Russian-language resource alone.

For services, the practical rule is to plan around practice when a person tells you it matters. Offer an appointment time that avoids prayer or Sabbath. Move a visit during Ramadan when a family asks. Honor a request for a same-gender interpreter or worker for intimate personal care when you can. Record these as scheduling and service facts, not as a religious profile.

Antisemitism and anti-Muslim hostility are real in Minnesota, from vandalism to threats against houses of worship to harassment at work. Organizations such as the Jewish Community Relations Council of Minnesota and the Dakotas and the Minnesota chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations offer education and track incidents. They are resources, not spokespeople for any individual, and imams and rabbis are not part of a case plan unless a person asks. Staff who are Muslim or Jewish are colleagues, not the curriculum; do not ask them to explain their religion on behalf of everyone.
lessons.keyPoint: Muslim and Jewish Minnesotans are diverse in origin, tradition and observance. Plan around practice when the person asks, and treat hostility toward either group as a safety and service issue.
lessons.example: Fictional case: Rachel manages a contract review with a provider agency. The on-site review is set for a Friday afternoon in late autumn and is expected to run past five. The agency director, Yosef, emails to say he must leave by three to be home before Shabbat, and asks whether a colleague can finish the review. Rachel's supervisor, Tom, suggests the director is trying to avoid scrutiny. Rachel checks and sees that nothing in the review requires the director personally after three.
lessons.question: What should Rachel do next?
choices: Offer to start earlier, or to finish the remaining items with the colleague or on another day, and note the change as a scheduling adjustment.
Keep the schedule, because changing it for one provider would be unfair to others.
Ask Yosef to confirm that he is observant before agreeing to any change.
feedback: This is the strongest response. The review's purpose is unchanged, the request is handled as ordinary scheduling, and no one's faith is questioned.
Fairness in oversight is about the standard, not the clock. Refusing a workable change adds a burden without improving the review.
Asking someone to prove their observance is intrusive and unnecessary for a routine scheduling request.
lessons.reflection: Which religious holidays or practices are built into your team's default calendar, and which ones do you have to look up? What does that tell you about whose schedule is treated as normal?
lessons.action: Add a reputable interfaith calendar to your team's shared planning resources, and before your next major meeting or deadline, check it for dates that could conflict with common observances.

check.question: Which statement best describes Muslim Minnesotans?
check.correct: They come from many backgrounds and traditions, and practice varies from person to person.
wrong: They are almost all Somali, so Somali community resources are the right starting point.
They all pray at work at fixed times, so every Muslim employee needs the same schedule.
check.feedback: Muslim Minnesotans include people of many origins and several traditions, and observance varies. Ethnicity and practice cannot be read from religion, so ask the person what matters for their services or work.

lessons.title: Traditional healing and ceremony, and people who are secular or have left religion
objectives: Explain why Dakota and Anishinaabe ceremony is connected to Tribal nationhood and government-to-government relations.
Distinguish traditional healing practices from different communities rather than grouping them together.
Describe the range of people who are unaffiliated, secular or have left a religion.
Identify what staff should not do when ceremony, healers or clergy come up in services.
lessons.teaching:
Minnesota shares geography with eleven federally recognized Tribal nations, seven Anishinaabe and four Dakota, and many Native people live in the Twin Cities and other urban areas. For Dakota and Anishinaabe people, ceremony and traditional healing are connected to language, land and nationhood. For much of American history, federal policy suppressed Native religious practice. The American Indian Religious Freedom Act later declared it United States policy to protect and preserve the right of American Indians to believe, express and exercise their traditional religions, including access to sites, use of sacred objects and freedom to worship through ceremonies. Many Native households also practice Christianity, sometimes together with traditional ways. When DHS work touches Tribal nations as governments, it goes through Tribal consultation, which is government-to-government. When an individual or family names a healer or ceremony, listen and follow their lead. Do not schedule ceremony as agency programming, do not describe it in a training as a recipe, and do not treat it as a team-building activity.

Other communities have their own healing traditions, and they are not interchangeable. A Hmong family may involve a txiv neeb, a shaman, in decisions about illness or disability. A Somali family may seek ruqya, Qur'anic recitation for healing. Latino, West African and Caribbean families may draw on other practices. Grouping these together as alternative medicine erases their meaning. The question for staff is practical: is there anyone or anything the person wants to include, and how can the service plan make room for it safely and respectfully.

About three in ten Minnesota adults describe themselves as religiously unaffiliated. That group includes atheists, agnostics, people who are spiritual but not religious, people who simply do not attend, and people who have left a faith, sometimes at real cost. A secular Jew, a former Muslim and an unaffiliated Black Minnesotan are not one category. Leaving a congregation is not leaving a family or people, and many households still keep holidays as kinship.

For all of these, the same boundaries apply. Do not assume that a person needs a pastor, imam, rabbi or healer, and do not assume they want none. Do not describe a lack of religion as a lack of culture or support. Ask, record what the person says, and let them decide who belongs in the room.
lessons.keyPoint: Ceremony and traditional healing belong to nations, families and communities, not to agency programming. Unaffiliated people are a large and varied group; never assign clergy or assume an absence of meaning.
lessons.example: Fictional case: Nicole is a DSD policy specialist drafting a guide on culturally responsive services for waiver case managers. A colleague, Brent, proposes a section titled Native healing practices that describes a sweat lodge step by step, based on a website he found, and suggests case managers offer to arrange one. Nicole knows the guide will affect services for Anishinaabe and Dakota people and for urban Native families, and that DHS has a Tribal consultation process and a Tribal liaison.
lessons.question: What should Nicole do next?
choices: Keep Brent's section but add a note that practices vary between Tribes.
Remove the step-by-step description, rewrite the section around asking and following the person's lead, and bring the draft to the Tribal liaison to determine what consultation it needs.
Delete all references to Native people so that the guide avoids any risk.
feedback: A caveat does not fix the problem. Describing ceremony as a procedure and offering to arrange it treats sacred practice as agency programming.
This is the strongest response. It removes extracted material, keeps the focus on the person's choices, and routes the policy question through the responsible government-to-government process.
Erasing Native people from a guide that affects their services is its own harm and skips the consultation the work requires.
lessons.reflection: When someone tells you they are not religious, what do you tend to assume about their values or support? When someone names a healer you do not know, what is your first reaction?
lessons.action: Find out who the Tribal liaison is for your part of DHS and how Tribal consultation is started. Save that contact where you keep your policy or planning resources.

check.question: What does the American Indian Religious Freedom Act state as federal policy?
check.correct: To protect and preserve the right of American Indians to believe, express and exercise their traditional religions, including access to sites, sacred objects and ceremonies.
wrong: To allow state agencies to offer Native ceremonies as part of public programs.
To replace Tribal consultation with individual consent for policy decisions.
check.feedback: The act declares a federal policy of protecting Native religious freedom, including sites, objects and ceremonies. It does not make ceremony a public program, and it does not replace the government-to-government consultation that policy affecting Tribal nations requires.

lessons.title: Practice: calendars, food, accommodation and respectful questions
objectives: Plan meetings and deadlines with a calendar that accounts for major religious observances.
Arrange food for work events so that people with religious dietary practices can take part.
Explain the basic duty to accommodate religious practice under Title VII and the Minnesota Human Rights Act, and route requests to Human Resources.
Draft respectful service questions that invite, but never require, information about faith.
lessons.teaching:
Faith shows up at work in ordinary ways. A training is scheduled on a major holiday. A team lunch offers only pork sandwiches. A colleague needs a quiet place and a few minutes to pray. A family cannot meet on a Saturday. None of these needs a debate about religion. They need planning.

Start with the calendar. Before setting major meetings, public hearings, training days or deadlines, check an interfaith calendar for major observances such as Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha, Good Friday and Easter, Diwali and Lunar New Year. Some dates move each year. You will not avoid every observance, but you can avoid the largest conflicts and offer alternatives. For food, label ingredients, include vegetarian choices, avoid making pork or alcohol the only option, and ask attendees in advance about dietary needs without asking why.

Religious accommodation at work is a legal duty. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act requires employers to reasonably accommodate an employee's sincerely held religious beliefs and practices unless doing so would cause undue hardship. After a recent Supreme Court decision, Groff v. DeJoy, the EEOC explains that undue hardship means a burden that is substantial in the overall context of the employer's business, not merely a small cost. Common accommodations include flexible scheduling, voluntary shift swaps, prayer breaks and exceptions to dress and grooming rules. The Minnesota Human Rights Act also protects employees from religious discrimination, and the Minnesota Department of Human Rights notes that state law gives public employees days off for religious holidays that do not fall on a Sunday or legal holiday; that time is unpaid unless the employee uses leave or makes up the hours. Supervisors should respond promptly and involve Human Resources, which decides formal requests. Requesting a religious accommodation is protected activity, so it must never count against someone.

In services, invite rather than require. A useful question is: Are there any beliefs, practices, days or people you would like us to keep in mind as we plan your services? Accept any answer, including none, and do not probe. If a person asks for a faith leader, healer or community organization to be involved, ask what role they want that person to play. Record requests as preferences in the person's own words. When a formal service or civil rights question arises, point to the right office, such as Human Resources, the Equal Opportunity and Access Division or legal counsel.
lessons.keyPoint: Most faith needs at work and in services are planning tasks. Check the calendar, plan the food, route accommodation requests to Human Resources, and ask open questions that anyone can answer with none.
lessons.example: Fictional case: Paul supervises a DSD unit and is planning a full-day team retreat with lunch. Two weeks before, a team member, Hodan, tells him the date falls on Eid al-Fitr and she had planned to take leave. Another team member, Lars, asks whether the retreat could include a short prayer before lunch, as his previous office did. Paul wants everyone to attend and feel welcome, and the retreat date was chosen mainly because the room was free.
lessons.question: What should Paul do next?
choices: Keep the date and open the lunch with a short, general prayer so everyone feels included.
Keep the date and tell Hodan that she can read the notes afterward.
Check whether the retreat can move, plan food everyone can eat, and keep the event free of group prayer while respecting anyone's private practice.
feedback: A group prayer at a work event pressures people of other faiths and none, and it does not address the conflict with Eid.
Hodan would miss a team event because of the calendar, even though the date was chosen for convenience. That is avoidable exclusion.
This is the strongest response. It removes an avoidable conflict, makes lunch inclusive and keeps a public workplace neutral while leaving room for private practice.
lessons.reflection: Think about the last work event you planned or attended. Who might have found it harder to take part because of the date, the food or the format?
lessons.action: Before your next team event or major deadline, check an interfaith calendar, add a dietary needs question to the invitation, and note who in Human Resources handles religious accommodation requests for your unit.

check.question: Under Title VII, as the EEOC now explains it, when may an employer deny a religious accommodation for undue hardship?
check.correct: When the burden would be substantial in the overall context of the employer's business.
wrong: Whenever the accommodation would cost anything at all.
Whenever a coworker says they dislike the arrangement.
check.feedback: After Groff v. DeJoy, a minimal cost is not enough. The employer must show a substantial burden in context. Coworker dislike alone does not create undue hardship. Human Resources makes these determinations, so supervisors should route requests promptly.

cards.back: Faith is related to ethnicity and culture but not the same. Islam is not Somali, the Black Church is not all of Black life, and Lutheran is not an ethnicity.
People who describe their religion as atheist, agnostic or nothing in particular. About three in ten Minnesota adults in recent Pew data; a varied group, not an absence of culture.
A change to a work rule or schedule so an employee can practice a sincerely held belief, required under Title VII unless it causes substantial hardship. Human Resources decides formal requests.
Government-to-government engagement between the state and Tribal nations on policy that affects them. It is distinct from an individual's choices about ceremony or healing.

cards.front: Clergy are not the case plan
cards.back: A pastor, priest, imam, rabbi or healer takes part in services only in the role the person asks for.

aid.heading: Before a meeting or event
items: Check an interfaith calendar for major observances before setting dates.
Ask about dietary needs in the invitation without asking for reasons.
Offer vegetarian options and label ingredients; do not make pork or alcohol the only choice.
Keep work events free of group prayer while respecting private practice.

aid.heading: In services
items: Ask: Are there any beliefs, practices, days or people you would like us to keep in mind?
Accept any answer, including none, and do not probe.
Record preferences in the person's own words, not as a religious label.
If the person names a faith leader or healer, ask what role they want that person to play.

aid.heading: Route to the right office
items: Religious accommodation requests from employees go promptly to Human Resources.
Discrimination or harassment concerns go to the Equal Opportunity and Access Division.
Policy that affects Tribal nations goes through the Tribal liaison and consultation process.
Questions about legal duties go to legal counsel.

Small groups such as Jewish and Muslim adults cannot be estimated precisely; use as a dated snapshot, not a description of individuals.
